problem: Visual homing requires the home location to be inside the robot's field of view, which limits it to the locality of the goal; existing fixes (topological maps, Trailmap) need maintained shared maps, and prior multi-robot sharing uses point-to-point image transmission that scales poorly.
motivation: Visual homing is lightweight and works in GPS-denied or changing environments, so extending its range without a global map is valuable. A team of robots can supply up-to-date, path-specific intermediate landmarks, but this needs secure, scalable, decentralized sharing of panoramas.
key_idea: Robots write their panoramic views as transactions to a shared blockchain ledger, so a robot that cannot see its home can chain through other robots' shared common landmarks to reach it via successive visual homing.
insight: A blockchain ledger holding every robot's latest panorama in the last block allows cheap lookups of landmark chains (R1-R2-R3 to goal) instead of n^2 broadcast of images. Table results show update and retrieval latency stay nearly flat as positions grow from 40 to 500, and landmark quality (3.41/3.35/3.40) is unchanged versus the point-to-point scheme. The evidence is simulation timing only, with no navigation success evaluated.
method: Transaction: each robot creates a transaction (ID, hash, timestamp, panorama as a list of slightly overlapping images) when it moves past a distance threshold, its panorama changes by more than a threshold, or a time threshold elapses.

Ledger/block structure: SHA256-linked blocks holding previous hash, own hash, timestamp and all robots' transactions; unchanged transactions are carried over so the last block always has the latest panoramas of all robots.
Landmark-chain query: the robot looks in the last block for robots that see the goal, then finds a chain of robots sharing common landmarks with its own view (R1-R2, R2-R3).

Navigation via chained visual homing: home to the first common landmark, look around, identify the next landmark, home again, and finally home to the goal; assumes nearby landmarks are spatially grouped.
Landmark recognition: reuses the YOLO + SIFT common-landmark identification of Lyons and Petzinger (UCIC software) modified to use the blockchain.
Testbed: ROS/Gazebo simulation of a 130x180 m suburban area with two Pioneer P3AT robots placed 1-20 m apart.

setting.backbone: YOLO + SIFT landmark matching (from prior work) plus SHA256 blockchain ledger
setting.training_data: none reported (uses existing pretrained YOLO; no new training)
setting.observation: panoramic RGB from stitched overlapping camera images
setting.action_space: visual homing toward landmarks (no low-level action space specified)
setting.privileged: simulation model database used to score landmark quality; otherwise none

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark; results are ledger update/retrieval latency and landmark quality (Table 1: 40 pos: update 0.82998e-3 ms, retrieval 1.79e-5 ms, quality 3.41; 200 pos: 0.100515e-2 ms, 1.99e-5 ms, 3.35; 500 pos: 1.09e-3 ms, 1.98e-5 ms, 3.40).
results: In simulation with two robots, ledger update time is about 1e-3 ms and panorama retrieval about 2e-5 ms, essentially independent of the number of positions (40/200/500). Average landmark quality (3.35-3.41) shows no loss versus the point-to-point sharing of Lyons and Petzinger. No navigation success/SPL is reported.
limitations: Evaluated only with two robots in simulation and with latency/landmark-quality metrics; no end-to-end navigation success and no real robots
Latency figures ignore realistic network and consensus costs; ledger bloat, throughput and DoS are left as future work
Assumes landmarks are spatially grouped and that common landmarks exist between chained robots; the n^2 vs blockchain transmission claim is asserted, not measured
builds_on: Lyons and Petzinger (YOLO+SIFT common landmark identification)
compares_to: Lyons and Petzinger point-to-point image sharing
